  541:   The certificate records both rates, namely the block rate \(\tau_r\)
  542:   and the final output rate \(\theta_r\), together with
  543:   \(C_r,J_r,K_r,N_r\) and the explicit monotone-tail threshold. The
  544:   finitely many powers in the
  545:   residue class below that threshold are checked directly by rational
  546:   matrix powering and are included as exact inequalities; if necessary,
  547:   \(K_r\) is enlarged before the certificate is printed. Thus the
  548:   certificate verifies the displayed inequality for all
  549:   \(m\equiv r\bmod D_A\) with \(m\ge N_r\).
  550: 
  551:   Thus the verifier never appeals to an unnamed finite-chain formula.
  552:   Its normal form for each entry of \(P^m-S_r\) is the explicit finite
  553:   list consisting of the direct transient powers \(T^m\), the recurrent
  554:   return-error terms \(W_{j,t,a}E_{j,t+a}^h\), the residue-grouped
  555:   convolutions just displayed, and the geometric resolvent tails
  556:   \((I-T^{D_A})^{-1}T^u\). Each listed matrix is rational once the
  557:   stationary vectors and cyclic projections have been solved over
  558:   \(\QQ\), and each inequality is reduced to rational norm bounds plus
  559:   the certified root-isolation comparisons above.
  560: \end{proof}
  561: 
  562: \begin{theorem}[Algorithmic fixed-DFA prime-slice obstruction]
  563:   \label{thm:effective-fixed-dfa-prime-obstruction}
  564:   Fix \(b\ge2\) and a complete DFA
  565:   \(\mathcal A=(Q,\Sigma_b,\delta,q_0,F)\), encoded by its integer
  566:   transition table. Let \(B\) be its unlabeled transition matrix and
  567:   \(P=B/b\). There is an algorithm which outputs the following
  568:   compressed exact certificate.
  569:   \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
  570:     \item The transient set \(T\), the recurrent classes
  571:     \(R_1,\dots,R_s\) of \(P\), their periods \(d_j\), and cyclic
  572:     decompositions \(R_{j,0},\dots,R_{j,d_j-1}\).
  573:     \item For every \(j,t\), the stationary probability vector
  574:     \(\pi_{j,t}\) of the primitive return chain
  575:     \(P^{d_j}|_{R_{j,t}}\), with rational entries.
  576:     \item The absorption probabilities \(H_j(q)\), \(q\in T\), obtained
  577:     from
  578:     \[
  579:       (I-P_{TT})H_j=P_{T,R_j}\mathbf 1,
  580:     \]
  581:     and the refined cyclic absorption probabilities
  582:     \[
  583:       A_{j,t}(q)
  584:       :=\sum_{\ell\ge0}
  585:         e_q^{\mathsf T}P_{TT}^{\ell}P_{T,R_j}
  586:         S_{j,t+\ell+1}\mathbf 1 ,
  587:     \]
  588:     where indices are taken modulo \(d_j\) and
  589:     \(S_{j,u}\) is the cyclic projection onto \(R_{j,u}\).
  590:     Thus, conditional on absorption after \(\ell\) transient steps, the
  591:     recurrent entry class is chosen so that at every later time
  592:     \(m\equiv r\pmod {d_j}\) the recurrent chain lies in
  593:     \(R_{j,t+r}\). The displayed series is evaluated exactly as a
  594:     finite family of linear solves after grouping \(\ell\) modulo
  595:     \(d_j\), namely
  596:     \[
  597:       A_{j,t}
  598:       =
  599:       \sum_{u=0}^{d_j-1}
  600:       (I-P_{TT}^{d_j})^{-1}P_{TT}^uP_{T,R_j}
  601:       S_{j,t+u+1}\mathbf 1 .
  602:     \]
  603:     \item For each residue \(r\) modulo
  604:     \(D_A=\operatorname{lcm}_j d_j\), the compressed formula
  605:     \[
  606:       c_r=
  607:       \sum_{j=1}^s\sum_{t=0}^{d_j-1}
  608:       \alpha_{j,t}^{(r)}\,
  609:       \pi_{j,t+r}(F\cap R_{j,t+r}),
  610:       \tag{\(*\)}
  611:       \label{eq:compressed-cr}
  612:     \]
  613:     where
  614:     \[
  615:       \alpha_{j,t}^{(r)}=
  616:       \begin{cases}
  617:         1, & q_0\in R_{j,t},\\
  618:         A_{j,t}(q_0), & q_0\in T,\\
  619:         0, & \text{otherwise.}
  620:       \end{cases}
  621:     \]
  622:     Again all cyclic indices are read modulo \(d_j\). This formula
  623:     decides \(c_r=0\) or \(c_r>0\) by exact rational arithmetic.
  624:     \item Rational constants \(0<\tau_r<\theta_r<1\), \(K_r>0\), and
  625:     integer thresholds \(N_r\) such that
  626:     \[
  627:       \abs{a_m(\mathcal A)/b^m-c_r}\le K_r\theta_r^m
  628:       \qquad(m\equiv r\pmod {D_A},\ m\ge N_r).
  629:     \]
  630:     Here \(\tau_r\) is the certified decay rate for the transient and
  631:     return-error blocks, while \(\theta_r\) is the larger final
  632:     exponential rate after the polynomial convolution factor has been
  633:     absorbed. The certificate records the strict spectral-radius
  634:     inequalities and rational resolvent bounds of
  635:     \Cref{lem:effective-spectral-constants}, including the rational
  636:     numbers \(\tau_r,\theta_r\), rational upper bounds \(K_r\), the
  637:     monotone tail threshold, and the finite list of exact rational
  638:     inequalities checked before the tail. These data are enough to
  639:     verify the inequality mechanically, without reconstructing an
  640:     algebraic Jordan basis.
  641:   \end{enumerate}
  642:   \smallskip
  643:   \noindent\textit{Certificate schema.}
  644:   For each residue class the certificate schema consists of the
  645:   following fields, all represented by rational data except for the
  646:   root-isolation rectangles.
  647:   \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
  648:     \item Rational matrices \(P,T,Q_{j,t},E_{j,t}=Q_{j,t}-\Pi_{j,t}\),
  649:     the cyclic projections \(S_{j,t}\), and the rational vectors
  650:     \(\pi_{j,t},A_{j,t}\) solving the displayed linear systems.
  651:     The norm convention throughout the schema is the
  652:     \(\ell^\infty\) operator norm, i.e. maximum absolute row sum.
  653:     \item Rational numbers \(c_r,\tau_r,\theta_r,K_r,C_r\), integers
  654:     \(J_r,N_r\), and a tail threshold \(N_r^{\mathrm{tail}}\), with
  655:     \(0<\tau_r<\theta_r<1\).
  656:     \item Root-isolation certificates for every characteristic
  657:     polynomial: rational rectangles, each containing exactly one complex
  658:     root and disjoint from the others, whose squared-modulus intervals
  659:     certify \(\rho(T)<\tau_r\) and
  660:     \(\rho(E_{j,t})<\tau_r^{d_j}\). The verifier checks these by
  661:     Sturm--subdivision or any equivalent exact rational root-counting
  662:     procedure on the rectangles and by rational interval arithmetic for
  663:     the squared moduli.
  664:     \item Resolvent certificates
  665:     \((\gamma_A,\delta_A,U_A,L_A)\) for
  666:     \(A\in\{T\}\cup\{E_{j,t}\}_{j,t}\), with
  667:     \(\rho(A)<\gamma_A<\tau_r\) for \(A=T\) and
  668:     \(\rho(A)<\gamma_A<\tau_r^{d_j}\) for \(A=E_{j,t}\). The verifier
  669:     checks, using the same isolating rectangles and rational interval
  670:     arithmetic, that every rectangle lies strictly inside the circle
  671:     \(|z|=\gamma_A\) and supplies a positive rational distance
  672:     \(\Delta_\xi\) from the rectangle to that circle. Therefore
  673:     \[
  674:       |\det(zI-A)|\ge \prod_{\xi}\Delta_\xi=:\delta_A
  675:       \qquad(|z|=\gamma_A),
  676:     \]
  677:     with roots counted with algebraic multiplicity. The verifier also
  678:     checks the elementary coefficient bound
  679:     \[
  680:       \|\operatorname{adj}(zI-A)\|_\infty\le U_A,
  681:     \]
  682:     and hence that \(\|A^n\|_\infty\le L_A\gamma_A^n\) for all
  683:     \(n\ge0\).
  684:     \item A rational block-form expansion of \(P^m-S_r\) on the residue
  685:     class \(m\equiv r\pmod {D_A}\). For every recurrent block \(R_j\)
  686:     and residue \(a\bmod d_j\) the data include the rational cyclic step
  687:     matrices \(G_{j,u}=P_{R_{j,u},R_{j,u+1}}\), their products
  688:     \(W_{j,t,a}=G_{j,t}\cdots G_{j,t+a-1}\), the rational limit matrix
  689:     \(C_{j,a}^{\infty}\), and the checked identities
  690:     \[
  691:       C_j^{d_jh+a}-C_{j,a}^{\infty}
  692:       =
  693:       \sum_t M_{j,t,a}(h)
  694:     \]
  695:     for \(h\ge1\). Here \(M_{j,t,a}(h)\) is zero except on the
  696:     \(R_{j,t}\)-to-\(R_{j,t+a}\) block, where it equals
  697:     \(W_{j,t,a}E_{j,t+a}^h\). The finitely many \(h=0\) cases are
  698:     checked directly. For every block from the transient part to \(R_j\),
  699:     the data also include the exact identity
  700:     \[
  701:       (P^m-S_r)_{T,R_j}
  702:       =
  703:       \sum_{\ell=0}^{m-1}
  704:         T^\ell P_{T,R_j}
  705:         \bigl(C_j^{m-1-\ell}-C_{j,r-\ell-1}^{\infty}\bigr)
  706:       -
  707:       \sum_{\ell=m}^{\infty}
  708:         T^\ell P_{T,R_j}C_{j,r-\ell-1}^{\infty}.
  709:     \]
  710:     These are finite rational identities: the second infinite sum is
  711:     verified after grouping \(\ell\bmod D_A\) as a finite list of
  712:     geometric resolvents \((I-T^{D_A})^{-1}T^u\). The verifier checks
  713:     each displayed identity by rational matrix multiplication and exact
  714:     inversion over \(\QQ\). For the first finite convolution, the
  715:     verifier further splits \(\ell=u+D_Aq\). If the recurrent factor in
  716:     that residue has length \(m-1-\ell=d_jh+a\), with
  717:     \(0\le a<d_j\), then
  718:     \[
  719:       h=H_{m,u}-L_jq,\qquad
  720:       L_j:=D_A/d_j,\qquad
  721:       H_{m,u}:=(m-1-u-a)/d_j .
  722:     \]
  723:     The integer \(a\) is fixed by the listed residue class, so
  724:     \(H_{m,u}\) is integral and the return-error exponent decreases as
  725:     \(q\) increases. The certificate records only the terms with
  726:     \(H_{m,u}-L_jq\ge1\); the finitely many smaller recurrent exponents
  727:     are moved to the direct finite-check list. The resulting finite
  728:     residue list is
  729:     \[
  730:       \sum_{q=0}^{Q(m,u)}
  731:         X_{u}T^{D_Aq}Y_{u}E_{j,t_u}^{H_{m,u}-L_jq}Z_{u},
  732:     \]
  733:     with all matrices \(X_u,Y_u,Z_u\) rational. This is the normal form
  734:     for every convolution term.
  735:     \item The exact convolution bounds attached to the preceding
  736:     expansion. For every direct term \(X A^nY\) the certificate lists
  737:     the rational product
  738:     \(\|X\|_\infty L_A\|Y\|_\infty\eta^n\). For every convolution term
  739:     it lists the rational coefficient
  740:     \[
  741:       C_u=\|X_u\|_\infty L_T\|Y_u\|_\infty
  742:         L_{E_{j,t_u}}\|Z_u\|_\infty\tau_r^{-1-u-a}
  743:     \]
  744:     for the corresponding residue \(u,a\); if \(a=0\), this means the
  745:     same displayed formula with the factor \(\tau_r^{-1-u}\). Indeed
  746:     \(T^{D_Aq}\) contributes at most \(\tau_r^{D_Aq}\), while
  747:     \(E_{j,t_u}^{H_{m,u}-L_jq}\) contributes at most
  748:     \(\tau_r^{d_jH_{m,u}-D_Aq}\); the \(q\)-dependence cancels, and the
  749:     identity \(m-1-u=d_jH_{m,u}+a\) gives
  750:     \[
  751:       \tau_r^{D_Aq}\tau_r^{d_jH_{m,u}-D_Aq}
  752:       =\tau_r^{m-1-u-a},
  753:     \]
  754:     which is bounded by the displayed \(C_u\tau_r^m\) coefficient for
  755:     each \(q\). The number of terms is at most \(m\),
  756:     so the residue summand is bounded by \(C_um\tau_r^m\). For every
  757:     tail it lists the
  758:     rational coefficient in
  759:     \(C\,\tau_r^m/(1-\tau_r^{D_A})\). Summing these finitely many
  760:     coefficients gives the stated coefficient bound
  761:     proving
  762:     \[
  763:       \|P^m-S_r\|_\infty\le C_rm^{J_r}\tau_r^m
  764:       \qquad(m\equiv r\pmod {D_A}).
  765:     \]
  766:     \item The rational tail inequality
  767:     \[
  768:       C_rm^{J_r}\tau_r^m\le K_r\theta_r^m
  769:       \qquad(m\ge N_r^{\mathrm{tail}})
  770:     \]
  771:     and exact rational matrix-power checks for every
  772:     \(m<N_r^{\mathrm{tail}}\) in the residue class that is not covered
  773:     by the tail. The displayed exponential estimate is accepted with
  774:     \(N_r\) no smaller than both the finite-check cutoff and
  775:     \(N_r^{\mathrm{tail}}\).
  776:   \end{enumerate}
  777:   \smallskip
  778:   \noindent\textit{Certificate-verifier theorem.}
  779:   Given the fields just listed, there is a finite verifier which accepts
  780:   if and only if the following rational assertions all check:
  781:   the stochastic block decomposition is a permutation of \(P\); each
  782:   \(C_{j,a}^{\infty}\), \(\pi_{j,t}\), and \(A_{j,t}\) satisfies its
  783:   displayed linear equations; the root-isolation rectangles prove the
  784:   strict spectral-radius inequalities; the resolvent certificates prove
  785:   the listed bounds for every decaying block; the finite block normal
  786:   form for \(P^m-S_r\) is exactly the one displayed in the preceding
  787:   two items; the summed direct, convolution, and tail coefficients give
  788:   \(\|P^m-S_r\|_\infty\le C_rm^{J_r}\tau_r^m\) on the residue class;
  789:   the finitely many pre-tail powers satisfy the same advertised
  790:   estimate after enlargement of \(K_r\); and the rational monotone-tail
  791:   inequality gives \(C_rm^{J_r}\tau_r^m\le K_r\theta_r^m\). All steps
  792:   use rational matrix arithmetic, exact inverses over \(\QQ\), finite
  793:   root counts in rational rectangles, and rational interval arithmetic.
  794:   No unlisted block formula or limiting argument is part of the
  795:   verification step.
  796:   With this output, the following holds for every
  797:   \(m\ge M_r\) satisfying \(m\equiv r\pmod {D_A}\).
  798:   If \(c_r=0\), then
  799:   \[
  800:     a_m(\mathcal A)\le K_r\theta_r^m b^m
  801:     \quad\text{and}\quad
  802:     \abs{(L(\mathcal A)\cap\Sigma_b^m)\triangle\mathcal P_m^{(b)}}
  803:     \ge \frac{A_b}{2}\,\frac{b^m}{m}.
  804:   \]
  805:   If \(c_r>0\), then
  806:   \[
  807:     a_m(\mathcal A)\ge \frac{c_r}{2}b^m,
  808:     \qquad
  809:     \mathrm{Prec}_m\le \frac{2B_b}{c_r}\,\frac1m,
  810:   \]
  811:   whenever \(\mathrm{Prec}_m\) is defined, i.e. on lengths where the
  812:   denominator is nonzero, and
  813:   \[
  814:     \abs{(L(\mathcal A)\cap\Sigma_b^m)\triangle\mathcal P_m^{(b)}}
  815:     \ge \frac{c_r}{4} b^m .
  816:   \]
  817:   Here \(A_b,B_b,M_b\) may be the explicit constants supplied by
  818:   \Cref{lem:base-prime-count}. Consequently
  819:   one computes constants \(c_{\mathcal A,b}>0\) and \(M_{\mathcal A,b}\)
  820:   such that
  821:   \[
  822:     \abs{(L(\mathcal A)\cap\Sigma_b^m)\triangle\mathcal P_m^{(b)}}
  823:     \ge c_{\mathcal A,b}\,\frac{b^m}{m}
  824:     \qquad(m\ge M_{\mathcal A,b}).
  825:   \]
  826:   The compressed output is the tuple
  827:   \[
  828:     \mathcal C=(D_A,\{R_j,d_j,(R_{j,t})_t,\pi_{j,t},A_{j,t}\}_{j,t},
  829:       \{c_r,\tau_r,\theta_r,K_r,C_r,J_r,N_r,M_r\}_{r\bmod D_A})
  830:   \]
  831:   when all residues are enumerated. If \(D_A\) is large, the same data
  832:   may instead be represented by the class list together with an exact
  833:   residue-evaluation procedure for
  834:   \(r\mapsto c_r,\tau_r,\theta_r,K_r,C_r,J_r,N_r,M_r\) and the
  835:   corresponding proof object from part~\textup{(e)};
  836:   any final all-large constant obtained by taking a minimum over
  837:   residues is then represented by this finite minimization procedure.
  838:   Printing the full residue table is charged to output size \(D_A\).
  839:   No polynomial bound in the input size alone is asserted for the
  840:   spectral certificate, for enumerating all residues, or for the final
  841:   minimization.
  842: \end{theorem}
  843: 
  844: \begin{proof}
  845:   Compute the matrix \(B=\sum_{d\in\Sigma_b}T_d\), the stochastic matrix
  846:   \(P=B/b\), the transient set, the recurrent classes, their periods,
  847:   their cyclic decompositions, and the common period \(D_A\) by standard
  848:   graph algorithms. The vectors \(\pi_{j,t}\) are the unique solutions
  849:   of
  850:   \[
  851:     \pi_{j,t}P^{d_j}|_{R_{j,t}}=\pi_{j,t},
  852:     \qquad
  853:     \pi_{j,t}\mathbf 1=1.
  854:   \]
  855:   Because \(P\) has rational entries, these vectors are rational and
  856:   are obtained by rational Gaussian elimination. The absorption
  857:   probabilities \(H_j\) solve the displayed systems in the statement;
  858:   the matrix \(I-P_{TT}\) is invertible because \(T\) is transient.
  859:   For the cyclic refinements, group the defining series for
  860:   \(A_{j,t}\) by \(\ell\equiv u\pmod{d_j}\). Each group is a
  861:   rational expression in
  862:   \[
  863:     (I-P_{TT}^{d_j})^{-1}P_{TT}^uP_{T,R_j}S_{j,t+u+1}\mathbf 1,
  864:   \]
  865:   hence is again computed by exact rational linear algebra. Formula
  866:   \eqref{eq:compressed-cr} is precisely the canonical block-power limit
  867:   of \(u^{\mathsf T}P^m v\) along \(m\equiv r\pmod {D_A}\). Indeed,
  868:   suppose the chain starts in a transient state \(q\), remains
  869:   transient for exactly \(\ell\) steps, and then enters \(R_j\) at time
  870:   \(\ell+1\) in cyclic class \(R_{j,u}\). Because \(P\) maps
  871:   \(R_{j,a}\) into \(R_{j,a+1}\), at a later time
  872:   \(m\equiv r\pmod {d_j}\) its recurrent cyclic class is
  873:   \[
  874:     u+m-(\ell+1)\equiv u+r-\ell-1 \pmod {d_j}.
  875:   \]
  876:   To contribute to the limiting distribution
  877:   \(\pi_{j,t+r}\) on \(R_{j,t+r}\), the entry class must therefore
  878:   satisfy \(u+r-\ell-1\equiv t+r\), equivalently
  879:   \(u\equiv t+\ell+1\pmod {d_j}\). This is exactly the projection
  880:   \(S_{j,t+\ell+1}\) in the definition of \(A_{j,t}\). Conditioning on
  881:   the absorption time and then applying the primitive return-chain limit
  882:   on \(R_{j,t+r}\) proves \eqref{eq:compressed-cr}.
  883: 
  884:   Applying \Cref{lem:effective-spectral-constants} to \(P\) and
  885:   \(D_A\) gives \(\tau_r,\theta_r,K_r,N_r\) and
  886:   \[
  887:     \abs{a_m(\mathcal A)/b^m-c_r}\le K_r\theta_r^m
  888:     \qquad(m\equiv r\bmod {D_A},\ m\ge N_r).
  889:   \]
  890:   The associated certificate consists of rational
  891:   \(\tau_r,\theta_r,K_r,C_r\), the integer \(J_r\), the
  892:   spectral-radius proof objects for the transient and return-error
  893:   blocks, the rational resolvent bounds, the rational inequality
  894:   \(C_rm^{J_r}\tau_r^m\le K_r\theta_r^m\) on the tail, and the finite
  895:   rational power checks preceding the tail. Thus the quantified
  896:   inequality used below is part of the output, not an unverifiable
  897:   analytic side condition.
  898: 
  899:   Choose \(A_b,B_b>0\) and \(M_b\) from
  900:   \Cref{lem:base-prime-count}, so that
  901:   \[
  902:     A_b\,\frac{b^m}{m}
  903:     \le\abs{\mathcal P_m^{(b)}}
  904:     \le B_b\,\frac{b^m}{m}
  905:     \qquad(m\ge M_b).
  906:   \]
  907:   If \(c_r=0\), take \(M_r\ge \max(M_b,N_r)\) to be any integer in the
  908:   residue class tail satisfying
  909:   \[
  910:     K_r\theta_r^m\le \frac{A_b}{2m}
  911:     \qquad(m\ge M_r,\ m\equiv r\bmod {D_A}).
  912:   \]
  913:   Since \(K_r\) and \(\theta_r\) are rational, this threshold is
  914:   obtained by checking finitely many values before monotonicity of
  915:   \(mK_r\theta_r^m\) begins and then recording the first value after
  916:   which the monotone tail is below \(A_b/2\).
  917:   For \(m\ge M_r\) with \(m\equiv r\bmod {D_A}\),
  918:   \[
  919:     a_m(\mathcal A)\le \frac{A_b}{2}\frac{b^m}{m},
  920:   \]
  921:   so the symmetric difference is at least
  922:   \(A_b b^m/(2m)\).
  923: 
  924:   If \(c_r>0\), take \(M_r\ge \max(M_b,N_r)\) so that
  925:   \[
  926:     K_r\theta_r^m\le c_r/2,
  927:     \qquad
  928:     B_b/m\le c_r/4
  929:   \]
  930:   for all \(m\ge M_r\) with \(m\equiv r\bmod {D_A}\). This is again a
  931:   rational monotone-tail check.
  932:   Then \(a_m(\mathcal A)\ge(c_r/2)b^m\), whence
  933:   \[
  934:     \mathrm{Prec}_m
  935:     \le\frac{\abs{\mathcal P_m^{(b)}}}{a_m(\mathcal A)}
  936:     \le\frac{2B_b}{c_r}\frac1m,
  937:   \]
  938:   and
  939:   \[
  940:     \abs{(L(\mathcal A)\cap\Sigma_b^m)\triangle\mathcal P_m^{(b)}}
  941:     \ge a_m(\mathcal A)-\abs{\mathcal P_m^{(b)}}
  942:     \ge \frac{c_r}{4}b^m.
  943:   \]
  944:   This proves the positive-density lower bound.
  945: 
  946:   Taking
  947:   \(M_{\mathcal A,b}:=\max_r M_r\) and the minimum over the finitely many
  948:   positive constants \(A_b/2\) and \(c_r/4\) appearing above gives the
  949:   final all-large-\(m\) constant after replacing \(c_r b^m/4\) by the
  950:   weaker \(c_r b^m/(4m)\) in the positive-density residue classes.
  951:   The output statement follows from strongly connected component and
  952:   period algorithms, exact rational linear algebra, root isolation for
  953:   the finitely many characteristic polynomials, and the certified
  954:   resolvent construction in \Cref{lem:effective-spectral-constants}.
  955:   The certificate is compressed by recurrent class and cyclic class.
  956:   Printing all residues, and taking the final minimum by enumeration,
  957:   are charged to the chosen output representation.
  958: \end{proof}
  959: 
  960: \begin{example}[Two explicit certificates]
  961:   \label{ex:base-ending-zero-certificate}
  962:   Let \(\mathcal A_0\) be the complete DFA over \(\Sigma_b\) accepting
  963:   exactly the non-empty words ending in \(0\). It has states
  964:   \(q_0,q_1\), initial state \(q_0\), accepting set \(\{q_1\}\), and
  965:   transitions
  966:   \[
  967:     \delta(q_i,0)=q_1,\qquad
  968:     \delta(q_i,d)=q_0\quad(1\le d\le b-1).
  969:   \]
  970:   Its unlabeled transition matrix and stochastic matrix are
  971:   \[
  972:     B=\begin{pmatrix} b-1&1\\ b-1&1\end{pmatrix},
  973:     \qquad
  974:     P=\begin{pmatrix} (b-1)/b&1/b\\ (b-1)/b&1/b\end{pmatrix}.
  975:   \]
  976:   There is one recurrent aperiodic class \(R_1=\{q_0,q_1\}\), no
  977:   transient state, \(d_1=D_A=1\), and
  978:   \[
  979:     \pi_{1,0}=\bigl((b-1)/b,\;1/b\bigr),\qquad
  980:     c_0=\pi_{1,0}(\{q_1\})=1/b.
  981:   \]
  982:   Since \(P^2=P\), one may take \(S_0=P\), \(N_0=1\), any rational
  983:   \(0<\tau_0<\theta_0<1\), and any rational \(K_0>0\) for the advertised
  984:   convergence estimate on all \(m\ge1\). Equivalently,
  985:   \(a_m(\mathcal A_0)=b^{m-1}\) and
  986:   \(a_m(\mathcal A_0)/b^m=1/b\) for every \(m\ge1\).
  987: 
  988:   Let \(A_b,B_b,M_b\) be the constants from
  989:   \Cref{lem:base-prime-count}. The positive-density branch of
  990:   \Cref{thm:effective-fixed-dfa-prime-obstruction} may therefore use the
  991:   explicit threshold
  992:   \[
  993:     M_0:=\left\lceil\max\{M_b,4bB_b\}\right\rceil .
  994:   \]
  995:   For every \(m\ge M_0\),
  996:   \[
  997:     \mathrm{Prec}_m
  998:     \le
  999:     \frac{\abs{\mathcal P_m^{(b)}}}{a_m(\mathcal A_0)}
 1000:     \le

 1027: 
 1028: We first establish the quantitative obstruction that drives both
 1029: corollaries below.
 1030: 
 1031: \begin{proposition}[Quantitative recall/precision obstruction]
 1032:   \label{prop:dfa-quantitative-obstruction}
 1033:   Set
 1034:   \[
 1035:     a_m(\mathcal A):=\abs{L(\mathcal A)\cap\Sigma_b^m},
 1036:   \]
 1037:   and define
 1038:   \[
 1039:     \mathrm{Rec}_m
 1040:     :=\frac{\abs{L(\mathcal A)\cap\mathcal P_m^{(b)}}}{\abs{\mathcal P_m^{(b)}}},
 1041:     \qquad
 1042:     \mathrm{Prec}_m
 1043:     :=\frac{\abs{L(\mathcal A)\cap\mathcal P_m^{(b)}}}{a_m(\mathcal A)}
 1044:   \]
 1045:   whenever \(a_m(\mathcal A)>0\). Suppose that there exist \(\delta>0\)
 1046:   and infinitely many integers \(m\) such that
 1047:   \(\mathrm{Rec}_m\ge \delta\) and \(\mathrm{Prec}_m\ge \delta\). Then
 1048:   on those lengths,
 1049:   \[
 1050:     \delta\,\abs{\mathcal P_m^{(b)}}
 1051:     \le \abs{L(\mathcal A)\cap\mathcal P_m^{(b)}}
 1052:     \le a_m(\mathcal A)
 1053:     \le \delta^{-1}\abs{L(\mathcal A)\cap\mathcal P_m^{(b)}}
 1054:     \le \delta^{-1}\abs{\mathcal P_m^{(b)}}.
 1055:   \]
 1056:   In particular, \(a_m(\mathcal A)\asymp b^m/m\) along infinitely many
 1057:   lengths, contradicting \Cref{thm:dfa-density-dichotomy}.
 1058: \end{proposition}
 1059: 
 1060: \begin{proof}
 1061:   The lower bound follows from
 1062:   \[
 1063:     \abs{L(\mathcal A)\cap\mathcal P_m^{(b)}}
 1064:     =\mathrm{Rec}_m\,\abs{\mathcal P_m^{(b)}}
 1065:     \ge \delta\,\abs{\mathcal P_m^{(b)}},
 1066:   \]
 1067:   and the upper bound follows from
 1068:   \[
 1069:     a_m(\mathcal A)
 1070:     =\frac{\abs{L(\mathcal A)\cap\mathcal P_m^{(b)}}}{\mathrm{Prec}_m}
 1071:     \le \delta^{-1}\abs{L(\mathcal A)\cap\mathcal P_m^{(b)}}
 1072:     \le \delta^{-1}\abs{\mathcal P_m^{(b)}}.
 1073:   \]
 1074:   By \Cref{lem:base-prime-count}, the displayed chain gives
 1075:   \(a_m(\mathcal A)\asymp b^m/m\) on an infinite set \(M\) of lengths.
 1076: 
 1077:   Let \(D_A\), \(c_0,\dots,c_{D_A-1}\), and \(\theta\) be supplied by
 1078:   \Cref{thm:dfa-density-dichotomy}. By the pigeonhole principle, some
 1079:   residue class \(r\bmod D_A\) contains infinitely many lengths from
 1080:   \(M\). Along this infinite subsequence the preceding bounds give
 1081:   positive constants \(K_1,K_2\) such that
 1082:   \[
 1083:     \frac{K_1}{m}\le \frac{a_m(\mathcal A)}{b^m}
 1084:     \le \frac{K_2}{m}.
 1085:   \]
 1086:   If \(c_r=0\), then the density dichotomy gives
 1087:   \(a_m(\mathcal A)/b^m=O(\theta^m)\) on \(m\equiv r\pmod {D_A}\), which is
 1088:   incompatible with \(K_1/m\) on an infinite subsequence. If \(c_r>0\),
 1089:   then \(a_m(\mathcal A)/b^m\ge c_r/2\) for all sufficiently large
 1090:   \(m\equiv r\pmod {D_A}\), which is incompatible with the upper bound
 1091:   \(K_2/m\). Both residue-class alternatives contradict the assumed
 1092:   infinite set \(M\).
 1093: \end{proof}
 1094: 
 1095: \begin{corollary}[Symmetric-difference lower bound for base-\(b\) primes]
 1096:   \label{cor:dfa-prime-symmetric-diff}
 1097:   Let \(L(\mathcal A)\subseteq\Sigma_b^\ast\) be recognised by a fixed
 1098:   DFA \(\mathcal A\). Then there exists \(c_{\mathcal A,b}>0\) such that
 1099:   \[
 1100:     \abs{(L(\mathcal A)\cap\Sigma_b^m)\triangle \mathcal P_m^{(b)}}
 1101:     \ge c_{\mathcal A,b}\,\frac{b^m}{m}
 1102:   \]
 1103:   for all sufficiently large \(m\). If \(a_m(\mathcal A)/b^m\) lies in
 1104:   the positive-density alternative of \Cref{thm:dfa-density-dichotomy},
 1105:   then along an infinite arithmetic progression of lengths one has the
 1106:   stronger bound
 1107:   \[
 1108:     \abs{(L(\mathcal A)\cap\Sigma_b^m)\triangle \mathcal P_m^{(b)}}\gg b^m.
 1109:   \]
 1110: \end{corollary}
 1111: 
 1112: \begin{proof}
 1113:   Let \(D_A\ge 1\), \(c_0,\dots,c_{D_A-1}\ge 0\), and \(\theta\in(0,1)\) be
 1114:   as in \Cref{thm:dfa-density-dichotomy}. Replacing \(\theta\) by
 1115:   \(\theta^{D_A}\) if necessary, we may write for each residue class
 1116:   \(r\bmod D_A\)
 1117:   \[
 1118:     \frac{a_{D_Ak+r}(\mathcal A)}{b^{D_Ak+r}}=c_r+O(\theta^k)
 1119:     \qquad (k\to\infty).
 1120:   \]
 1121:   Fix constants \(A_b,B_b>0\), supplied by
 1122:   \Cref{lem:base-prime-count}, such that
 1123:   \[
 1124:     A_b\,\frac{b^m}{m}\le \abs{\mathcal P_m^{(b)}}\le B_b\,\frac{b^m}{m}
 1125:   \]
 1126:   for all sufficiently large \(m\).
 1127: 
 1128:   We now treat each residue class separately.
 1129: 
 1130:   If \(c_r=0\), then
 1131:   \[
 1132:     a_{D_Ak+r}(\mathcal A)=O(\theta^k b^{D_Ak+r})
 1133:     =o\!\left(\frac{b^{D_Ak+r}}{D_Ak+r}\right).
 1134:   \]
 1135:   Hence there exists \(k_r\) such that for all \(k\ge k_r\),
 1136:   \[
 1137:     a_{D_Ak+r}(\mathcal A)
 1138:     \le \frac{A_b}{2}\,\frac{b^{D_Ak+r}}{D_Ak+r}.
 1139:   \]
 1140:   For those \(k\),
 1141:   \[
 1142:     \abs{(L(\mathcal A)\cap\Sigma_b^{D_Ak+r})\triangle \mathcal P_{D_Ak+r}^{(b)}}
 1143:     \ge \abs{\mathcal P_{D_Ak+r}^{(b)}}-a_{D_Ak+r}(\mathcal A)
 1144:     \ge \frac{A_b}{2}\,\frac{b^{D_Ak+r}}{D_Ak+r}.
 1145:   \]
 1146: 
 1147:   If \(c_r>0\), then there exists \(k_r\) such that for all \(k\ge k_r\),
 1148:   \[
 1149:     a_{D_Ak+r}(\mathcal A)\ge \frac{c_r}{2}\,b^{D_Ak+r}.
 1150:   \]
 1151:   Enlarging \(k_r\) if necessary, we may also ensure that
 1152:   \(B_b/(D_Ak+r)\le c_r/4\). Then for all such \(k\),
 1153:   \[
 1154:     \abs{(L(\mathcal A)\cap\Sigma_b^{D_Ak+r})\triangle \mathcal P_{D_Ak+r}^{(b)}}
 1155:     \ge a_{D_Ak+r}(\mathcal A)-\abs{\mathcal P_{D_Ak+r}^{(b)}}
 1156:     \ge \frac{c_r}{4}\,b^{D_Ak+r}.
 1157:   \]
 1158: 
 1159:   Since there are only finitely many residue classes, taking the minimum
 1160:   of \(A_b/2\) and the finitely many numbers \(c_r/4\) arising in the
 1161:   case \(c_r>0\) yields a constant \(c_{\mathcal A,b}>0\) such that
 1162:   \[
 1163:     \abs{(L(\mathcal A)\cap\Sigma_b^m)\triangle \mathcal P_m^{(b)}}
 1164:     \ge c_{\mathcal A,b}\,\frac{b^m}{m}
 1165:   \]
 1166:   for all sufficiently large \(m\). If \(a_m(\mathcal A)/b^m\) falls in
 1167:   the positive-density alternative of \Cref{thm:dfa-density-dichotomy},
 1168:   then some residue class has \(c_r>0\), and along that infinite
 1169:   arithmetic progression the stronger bound
 1170:   \(\abs{(L(\mathcal A)\cap\Sigma_b^m)\triangle \mathcal P_m^{(b)}}\gg b^m\)
 1171:   holds.
 1172: \end{proof}
 1173: 
 1174: \begin{remark}[Sharpness of the lower bounds]\label{rem:prime-diff-sharp}
 1175:   The two scales in \Cref{cor:dfa-prime-symmetric-diff} are optimal up
 1176:   to the implicit constants. If \(L=\emptyset\), then
 1177:   \[
 1178:     \abs{(L(\mathcal A)\cap\Sigma_b^m)\triangle\mathcal P_m^{(b)}}
 1179:     =\abs{\mathcal P_m^{(b)}}\asymp b^m/m .
 1180:   \]
 1181:   On the other hand, for the positive-density language
 1182:   \(\Sigma_b^\ast0\) the symmetric difference with
 1183:   \(\mathcal P_m^{(b)}\) is \(\asymp b^m\) along every residue class,
 1184:   so the strengthened \(\Omega(b^m)\) conclusion on arithmetic
 1185:   progressions cannot be improved.
 1186: \end{remark}
 1187: 
 1188: \begin{corollary}[No simultaneous recall and precision for fixed DFA]
 1189:   \label{cor:dfa-prime-recall-precision}
 1190:   With \(\mathrm{Rec}_m\) and \(\mathrm{Prec}_m\) as in
 1191:   \Cref{prop:dfa-quantitative-obstruction}, let \(D_A\) and
 1192:   \(c_0,\dots,c_{D_A-1}\) be the automaton period and residue constants supplied by
 1193:   \Cref{thm:dfa-density-dichotomy}. For each residue class
 1194:   \(r\bmod D_A\) exactly one of the following alternatives holds:
 1195:   \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
 1196:     \item If \(c_r=0\), then \(\mathrm{Rec}_m\) decays exponentially
 1197:     along \(m\equiv r\pmod {D_A}\).
 1198:     \item If \(c_r>0\), then there is a constant
 1199:     \(C_r=2B_b/c_r\), where
 1200:     \(\abs{\mathcal P_m^{(b)}}\le B_b b^m/m\) for all large \(m\),
 1201:     such that \(\mathrm{Prec}_m\le C_r/m\) for all sufficiently large
 1202:     \(m\equiv r\pmod {D_A}\) for which \(a_m(\mathcal A)>0\).
 1203:   \end{enumerate}
 1204:   Consequently every DFA satisfies one of the following statements:
 1205:   \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
 1206:     \item \(\mathrm{Rec}_m\to 0\) exponentially fast.
 1207:     \item There exists at least one residue class
 1208:     \(r\bmod D_A\) with \(c_r>0\) such that
 1209:     \(\mathrm{Prec}_m\le C_{\mathcal A,b}/m\) for all sufficiently large
 1210:     \(m\equiv r\pmod {D_A}\) for which precision is defined.
 1211:   \end{enumerate}
 1212:   Precision is left undefined on lengths with \(a_m(\mathcal A)=0\);
 1213:   no assertion is made about other positive-density or sparse residue
 1214:   classes beyond the per-residue alternatives above.
 1215:   In particular, no fixed DFA has both recall and precision bounded
 1216:   away from zero for infinitely many lengths.
 1217: \end{corollary}
 1218: 
 1219: \begin{proof}
 1220:   Apply \Cref{thm:dfa-density-dichotomy}. Thus there exist an integer
 1221:   \(D_A\ge 1\), constants \(c_0,\dots,c_{D_A-1}\ge 0\), and
 1222:   \(\theta\in(0,1)\) such that
 1223:   \[
 1224:     \frac{a_m(\mathcal A)}{b^m}=c_{m\bmod D_A}+O(\theta^m).
 1225:   \]
 1226:   Fix the upper-bound constant \(B_b>0\) from
 1227:   \Cref{lem:base-prime-count}, so that
 1228:   \(\abs{\mathcal P_m^{(b)}}\le B_b b^m/m\) for all sufficiently large
 1229:   \(m\).
 1230:   We treat each residue class \(r\bmod D_A\) separately by considering the
 1231:   two cases \(c_r=0\) and \(c_r>0\).
 1232: 
 1233:   \textit{Case \(c_r=0\).}
 1234:   Along the subsequence \(m\equiv r\pmod {D_A}\), we have
 1235:   \(a_m(\mathcal A)=O(\theta^m b^m)\). Since
 1236:   \Cref{lem:base-prime-count} gives
 1237:   \(\abs{\mathcal P_m^{(b)}}\asymp b^m/m\), so
 1238:   \[
 1239:     \mathrm{Rec}_m
 1240:     \le \frac{a_m(\mathcal A)}{\abs{\mathcal P_m^{(b)}}}
 1241:     \ll \theta^m\cdot m.
 1242:   \]
 1243:   Because \(m\theta^m=O(\theta_r^m)\) for some \(\theta_r\in(0,1)\),
 1244:   recall decays exponentially along this residue class.
 1245: 
 1246:   \textit{Case \(c_r>0\).}
 1247:   Along \(m\equiv r\pmod {D_A}\) with \(m\) large enough, we have
 1248:   \(a_m(\mathcal A)\ge \tfrac{1}{2}c_r b^m\). Using the bound for
 1249:   \(\abs{\mathcal P_m^{(b)}}\),
 1250:   \[
 1251:     \mathrm{Prec}_m
 1252:     \le \frac{\abs{\mathcal P_m^{(b)}}}{a_m(\mathcal A)}
 1253:     \le \frac{2B_b}{c_r}\cdot\frac{1}{m}.
 1254:   \]
 1255:   Hence precision decays at the rate \(O(1/m)\) along this
 1256:   arithmetic progression, so we may take
 1257:   \(C_{\mathcal A,b}=2B_b/c_r\) for that subsequence.
 1258: 
 1259:   Every residue class \(r\bmod D_A\) falls into one of these two cases.
 1260:   If all residue classes have \(c_r=0\), then
 1261:   \(\mathrm{Rec}_m\to 0\) exponentially for every \(m\), giving
 1262:   alternative~\textup{(i)}. Otherwise, at least one residue class has
 1263:   \(c_r>0\), and \(\mathrm{Prec}_m\le C_{\mathcal A,b}/m\) on defined
 1264:   lengths along that infinite arithmetic progression, giving
 1265:   alternative~\textup{(ii)}.
 1266: 
 1267:   If both recall and precision were bounded below by some
 1268:   \(\delta>0\) for infinitely many lengths, then
 1269:   \Cref{prop:dfa-quantitative-obstruction} would force
 1270:   \(a_m(\mathcal A)\asymp b^m/m\) along an infinite set of lengths. But the
 1271:   per-residue analysis above shows that on each residue class either
 1272:   \(a_m(\mathcal A)\) is exponentially sparse or \(a_m(\mathcal A)\gg b^m\), and
 1273:   neither is compatible with \(a_m(\mathcal A)\asymp b^m/m\).
 1274: \end{proof}
 1275: 
 1276: \subsection{Relative density for deterministic presentations}
 1277: 
 1278: We use the following deterministic presentation convention in the
 1279: relative-density statements.
 1280: 
 1281: \begin{definition}[Trim deterministic presentation]
 1282:   \label{def:trim-deterministic-presentation}
 1283:   A deterministic presentation over a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) is a
 1284:   tuple
 1285:   \[
 1286:     \mathcal N=(Q_N,\Sigma,\delta_N,q_N,F_N),
 1287:   \]
 1288:   where \(Q_N\) is finite, \(q_N\in Q_N\), \(F_N\subseteq Q_N\), and
 1289:   \(\delta_N:Q_N\times\Sigma\rightharpoonup Q_N\) is a partial
 1290:   transition map. A word is accepted if it labels a path from \(q_N\)
 1291:   to a state in \(F_N\). Its adjacency matrix is
 1292:   \[
 1293:     (B_N)_{qq'}
 1294:     :=\#\{a\in\Sigma:\delta_N(q,a)=q'\};
 1295:   \]
 1296:   thus several letters leading from \(q\) to the same state \(q'\) are
 1297:   counted with their multiplicity, while unavailable letters contribute
 1298:   no edge. The presentation is trim if every state is reachable from
 1299:   \(q_N\) and can reach some state of \(F_N\). It is strongly connected
 1300:   if the directed graph with edges \(q\to q'\) whenever
 1301:   \(\delta_N(q,a)=q'\) for some \(a\in\Sigma\) is strongly connected.
 1302: 
 1303:   If \(\mathcal A=(Q_A,\Sigma,\delta_A,q_A,F_A)\) is another
 1304:   deterministic automaton over the same alphabet, its synchronous
 1305:   product with \(\mathcal N\) has state set \(Q_N\times Q_A\), initial
 1306:   state \((q_N,q_A)\), accepting set \(F_N\times F_A\), and the partial
 1307:   transition
 1308:   \[
 1309:     (q,s)\xrightarrow{a}(\delta_N(q,a),\delta_A(s,a))
 1310:   \]
 1311:   exactly for letters \(a\) for which both displayed transitions are
 1312:   defined. Completing \(\mathcal A\) by a sink state, when desired, does
 1313:   not change the intersection language.
 1314: \end{definition}
 1315: 
 1316: We first record the finite-budget statement in the general
 1317: multicomponent form. This is the version needed when the deterministic
 1318: presentation is trim but its adjacency matrix has several maximal
 1319: strongly connected components, possibly connected by transient paths.
 1320: The polynomial factors in the statement are exactly the factors absent
 1321: from the strongly connected specialization below.
 1322: 
 1323: \noindent\textit{\(\lambda\)-active residues.}
 1324: Let \(\mathcal N\) be a trim deterministic presentation with adjacency
 1325: matrix \(B_N\), let \(\lambda=\rho(B_N)>1\), and let
 1326: \(z_m=\abs{L(\mathcal N)\cap\Sigma^m}\). After a period \(D\) has been
 1327: fixed, call a residue class \(r\bmod D\) \(\lambda\)-active if
 1328: \[
 1329:   z_m\not=O(\theta^m)
 1330:   \qquad (m\equiv r\pmod D)
 1331: \]
 1332: for every \(\theta<\lambda\). Equivalently, accepted words in that
 1333: residue class have exponential growth rate \(\lambda\). A residue class
 1334: can contain infinitely many accepted lengths without being
 1335: \(\lambda\)-active: in a reducible presentation those words may be
 1336: supplied only by components of smaller spectral radius. The
 1337: multicomponent theorem below separates this lower-growth phenomenon
 1338: from the Perron-scale comparison.
 1339: 
 1340: \begin{theorem}[Multicomponent finite-budget obstruction]
 1341:   \label{thm:multicomponent-finite-budget}
 1342:   Let \(\mathcal N\) be a trim deterministic presentation,
 1343:   not necessarily strongly connected, with adjacency matrix \(B_N\).
 1344:   Let \(\lambda:=\rho(B_N)>1\), and put
 1345:   \(z_m=\abs{L(\mathcal N)\cap\Sigma^m}\). Then there are an integer
 1346:   period \(D\ge1\), a number \(0<\theta<\lambda\), an integer
 1347:   \(S\ge0\), and, for every residue \(r\bmod D\), an exponent
 1348:   \(s_r\in\{-\infty,0,\dots,S\}\) and a constant \(d_r\ge0\) such that
 1349:   \(s_r\ge0\) and \(d_r>0\) exactly on the \(\lambda\)-active residue
 1350:   classes, while \(s_r=-\infty\) and \(d_r=0\) on all other residue
 1351:   classes. On every residue class
 1352:   \[
 1353:     z_m
 1354:     =
 1355:     \lambda^m
 1356:     \left(
 1357:       d_r m^{s_r}
 1358:       +O(m^{s_r-1})
 1359:     \right)
 1360:     +O(\theta^m m^S),
 1361:     \qquad m\equiv r\pmod D .
 1362:   \]
 1363:   The convention is that the \(O(m^{-1})\) term is absent when
 1364:   \(s_r=0\), and the displayed polynomial part is absent when
 1365:   \(s_r=-\infty\). Thus non-\(\lambda\)-active residue classes, even
 1366:   those with infinitely many accepted lengths, are absorbed into the
 1367:   sub-Perron error term.
 1368: 
 1369:   For every deterministic automaton \(\mathcal A\) over \(\Sigma\) and
 1370:   \[
 1371:     a_m(\mathcal A,\mathcal N)
 1372:     :=\abs{L(\mathcal A)\cap L(\mathcal N)\cap\Sigma^m},
 1373:   \]
 1374:   after replacing \(D,S,\theta\) by common choices, there are
 1375:   constants \(e_r\ge0\) and exponents
 1376:   \(t_r\in\{-\infty,0,\dots,S\}\) such that on every residue class
 1377:   \[
 1378:     a_m(\mathcal A,\mathcal N)
 1379:     =
 1380:     \lambda^m
 1381:     \left(
 1382:       e_r m^{t_r}
 1383:       +O(m^{t_r-1})
 1384:     \right)
 1385:     +O(\theta^m m^S),
 1386:   \]
 1387:   with the same convention when \(t_r=0\); if the intersection has
 1388:   exponential growth \(<\lambda\) on that residue, then \(t_r=-\infty\)
 1389:   and the first displayed polynomial part is absent. Moreover, whenever
 1390:   \(r\bmod D\) is \(\lambda\)-active, either \(t_r=-\infty\) or
 1391:   \(t_r\le s_r\), and if \(t_r=s_r\) then \(0\le e_r\le d_r\).
 1392: 
 1393:   Consequently, let \(T_m\subseteq L(\mathcal N)\cap\Sigma^m\) satisfy
 1394:   \[
 1395:     \alpha\frac{\lambda^m}{m}
 1396:     \le \abs{T_m}
 1397:     \le \beta\frac{\lambda^m}{m}
 1398:   \]
 1399:   for all sufficiently large \(m\) in every \(\lambda\)-active residue
 1400:   class, with fixed \(\alpha,\beta>0\). For every fixed deterministic automaton
 1401:   \(\mathcal A\) there is a constant
 1402:   \(C_{\mathcal A,\mathcal N,T}>0\) such that
 1403:   \[
 1404:     \abs{(L(\mathcal A)\cap L(\mathcal N)\cap\Sigma^m)\triangle T_m}
 1405:     \ge
 1406:     C_{\mathcal A,\mathcal N,T}\frac{\lambda^m}{m}
 1407:   \]
 1408:   for all sufficiently large \(m\) in \(\lambda\)-active residue
 1409:   classes. On each \(\lambda\)-active residue class either the recall
 1410:   against \(T_m\) tends to \(0\) exponentially or polynomially, or else
 1411:   the precision is \(O(1/m)\) whenever it is defined.
 1412: \end{theorem}
 1413: 
 1414: \begin{proof}
 1415:   Put \(B_N\) in Frobenius normal form. For a finite non-negative
 1416:   integer matrix, the rational generating function
 1417:   \(u_N^{\mathsf T}(I-xB_N)^{-1}v_N\) has poles at reciprocals of
 1418:   eigenvalues of \(B_N\), and the coefficients are finite sums of
 1419:   terms \(p_{\mu}(m)\mu^m\), where \(p_\mu\) is a polynomial whose
 1420:   degree is one less than the size of the largest Jordan block attached
 1421:   to \(\mu\), plus exponentially smaller terms. Equivalently, this is
 1422:   the Frobenius normal form or transfer-matrix expansion for regular
 1423:   languages; see \cite{SalomaaSoittola1978,BerstelReutenauer2011}.
 1424:   For a non-negative matrix, the eigenvalues of modulus \(\lambda\)
 1425:   that contribute to accepted paths are roots of unity times
 1426:   \(\lambda\), arising from maximal components and chains between them.
 1427:   Taking \(D\) to be a common period of those components makes the
 1428:   peripheral factors constant on each residue class. On a fixed residue
 1429:   \(r\bmod D\), look only at the terms whose exponential factor has
 1430:   modulus \(\lambda\). If no such term contributes to accepted paths in
 1431:   that residue, then the whole residue-class count has exponential
 1432:   growth \(<\lambda\); after enlarging \(\theta\) below \(\lambda\), it
 1433:   is included in \(O(\theta^m m^S)\), and we set \(s_r=-\infty\) and
 1434:   \(d_r=0\). This case includes residues with infinitely many accepted
 1435:   lengths supplied only by smaller components.
 1436: 
 1437:   If a Perron-scale term does contribute, collect the largest remaining
 1438:   polynomial degree as \(s_r\). The leading coefficient \(d_r\) is the
 1439:   sum of the non-negative leading contributions of maximal
 1440:   component-chains realizing that residue at that degree. This sum is
 1441:   positive, because at least one such Perron-scale chain contributes
 1442:   and no cancellation is possible for counts of paths in a
 1443:   non-negative matrix. These are precisely the \(\lambda\)-active
 1444:   residues, and the displayed expansion for \(z_m\) follows.
 1445: 
 1446:   Form the synchronous product of \(\mathcal N\) with \(\mathcal A\),
 1447:   trim unreachable or non-coaccessible states, and let \(B'\) be its
 1448:   adjacency matrix. Its accepted-word count is
 1449:   \(a_m(\mathcal A,\mathcal N)=u'^{\mathsf T}(B')^m v'\), so the same
 1450:   transfer-matrix expansion applies. Its exponential growth rate is at
 1451:   most \(\lambda\), because every accepted product word projects
 1452:   injectively to a word of \(L(\mathcal N)\). If the product growth rate
 1453:   is \(<\lambda\) on a residue class, it is absorbed into
 1454:   \(O(\theta^m m^S)\) after increasing \(\theta\) below \(\lambda\) and
 1455:   increasing \(S\). If the product has growth \(\lambda\), its leading
 1456:   polynomial degree on a \(\lambda\)-active residue cannot exceed \(s_r\);
 1457:   otherwise \(a_m(\mathcal A,\mathcal N)\le z_m\) would fail along that
 1458:   residue for large \(m\). The same inequality gives \(e_r\le d_r\)
 1459:   when \(t_r=s_r\).
 1460: 
 1461:   Fix a \(\lambda\)-active residue class and put
 1462:   \(A_m=L(\mathcal A)\cap L(\mathcal N)\cap\Sigma^m\). If
 1463:   \(t_r=-\infty\), then \(\abs{A_m}=O(\theta^m m^S)\), and hence
 1464:   \[
 1465:     \frac{\abs{A_m\cap T_m}}{\abs{T_m}}
 1466:     \le
 1467:     O(m^{S+1}(\theta/\lambda)^m),
 1468:   \]
 1469:   so recall decays exponentially and
 1470:   \(\abs{A_m\triangle T_m}\ge(\alpha/2)\lambda^m/m\) for all large
 1471:   \(m\) in the residue.
 1472: 
 1473:   Suppose next that the first non-zero leading term in the expansion of
 1474:   \(a_m(\mathcal A,\mathcal N)\) on this residue is
 1475:   \(\gamma_r\lambda^m m^{u_r}\), with \(\gamma_r>0\) and \(u_r\ge0\).
 1476:   Then, for all large \(m\) in the residue,
 1477:   \(\abs{A_m}\ge(\gamma_r/2)\lambda^m m^{u_r}\). Since
 1478:   \(\abs{T_m}\le\beta\lambda^m/m\),
 1479:   \[
 1480:     \abs{A_m\triangle T_m}
 1481:     \ge \abs{A_m}-\abs{T_m}
 1482:     \ge \frac{\gamma_r}{4}\lambda^m m^{u_r}
 1483:     \ge \frac{\gamma_r}{4}\frac{\lambda^m}{m},
 1484:   \]
 1485:   after enlarging the threshold. Whenever \(\abs{A_m}>0\),
 1486:   \[
 1487:     \frac{\abs{A_m\cap T_m}}{\abs{A_m}}
 1488:     \le
 1489:     \frac{2\beta}{\gamma_r}\frac{1}{m^{u_r+1}}
 1490:     \le
 1491:     \frac{2\beta}{\gamma_r}\frac1m .
 1492:   \]
 1493:   If no such non-zero polynomial term exists, the residue is in the
 1494:   exponentially smaller case already handled. There are only finitely
 1495:   many \(\lambda\)-active residue classes, so taking the minimum of the
 1496:   positive constants obtained above proves the uniform finite-budget
 1497:   bound. The theorem makes no prime-scale conclusion on
 1498:   non-\(\lambda\)-active residues, where \(L(\mathcal N)\) itself has
 1499:   sub-Perron growth and a target of size \(\asymp\lambda^m/m\) cannot
 1500:   be a subset of \(L(\mathcal N)\cap\Sigma^m\) for all large \(m\).

 1503: No additional numeration-system formalism is needed for the next
 1504: theorem beyond such a trim deterministic presentation whose underlying

 1506: \(\mathcal N\) is the canonical presentation of a regular numeration
 1507: system. Write
 1508: \[
 1509:   \mathcal N_m:=L(\mathcal N)\cap\Sigma^m,
 1510:   \qquad
 1511:   z_m:=\abs{\mathcal N_m}.
 1512: \]
 1513: Let \(B_N\) be the adjacency matrix of \(\mathcal N\), let
 1514: \(\lambda:=\rho(B_N)>1\) be its spectral radius, and let \(d_N\ge 1\)

 1516: 
 1517: \begin{lemma}[Cyclic-class path threshold]
 1518:   \label{lem:cyclic-class-path-threshold}
 1519:   Let \(B\) be an irreducible non-negative integer matrix with period
 1520:   \(d\) and cyclic decomposition \(C_0,\dots,C_{d-1}\), indexed so that
 1521:   \(B\) maps \(C_i\) to \(C_{i+1}\). For each pair of cyclic classes
 1522:   \(C_i,C_j\) there is an integer \(N_{ij}\) such that, whenever
 1523:   \(n\ge N_{ij}\) and \(n\equiv j-i\pmod d\), every pair
 1524:   \(x\in C_i\), \(y\in C_j\) is joined by at least one path of length
 1525:   \(n\). The threshold is uniform over the finite pair
 1526:   \(C_i\times C_j\).
 1527:   This is the elementary cyclic-class input used in the denominator
 1528:   positivity argument; it is not a separate contribution.
 1529: \end{lemma}
 1530: 
 1531: \begin{proof}
 1532:   The diagonal block of \(B^d\) on each cyclic class \(C_i\) is
 1533:   primitive. Hence for each \(i\) there is an exponent \(E_i\) such that
 1534:   \((B^{kd})_{xy}>0\) for every \(x,y\in C_i\) and every \(k\ge E_i\).
 1535:   If \(j-i\equiv h\pmod d\), irreducibility and the cyclic
 1536:   decomposition imply that for each \(x\in C_i\) and \(y\in C_j\) there
 1537:   is a path from \(x\) to \(y\) whose length is congruent to \(h\)
 1538:   modulo \(d\). Choose one such path for each finite pair and write its
 1539:   length as \(h+dq_{xy}\). Let \(Q_{ij}:=\max_{x,y}q_{xy}\), and let
 1540:   \(N_{ij}:=h+d(Q_{ij}+\max_iE_i)\), with
 1541:   \(h\in\{0,\dots,d-1\}\).
 1542: 
 1543:   For \(n=h+dk\ge N_{ij}\), use the chosen path
 1544:   \(x=x_0\to x_1\to\cdots\to x_{h+dq_{xy}}=y\). Its first \(h\) edges
 1545:   end at a state \(w\in C_j\). Since \(B^d|_{C_j}\) is primitive, there
 1546:   is a path of length \(d(k-q_{xy})\) from \(w\) to \(w\) whenever
 1547:   \(k-q_{xy}\ge E_j\). Follow the first \(h\) edges from \(x\) to \(w\),
 1548:   insert this return path at \(w\), and then follow the remaining
 1549:   \(dq_{xy}\) edges of the chosen path from \(w\) to \(y\). The total
 1550:   length is \(h+d(k-q_{xy})+dq_{xy}=n\).
 1551: \end{proof}
 1552: 
 1553: \begin{lemma}[Periodic growth of trim presentations]
 1554:   \label{lem:trim-density}
 1555:   With the notation above there exist \(d_N\) non-negative constants
 1556:   \(d_0,\dots,d_{d_N-1}\), at least one of which is positive, and
 1557:   \(\theta_N\in(0,1)\) such that
 1558:   \[
 1559:     z_m=\lambda^m\bigl(d_{m\bmod d_N}+O(\theta_N^m)\bigr)
 1560:     \qquad (m\to\infty).
 1561:   \]
 1562:   This is used only for trim strongly connected presentations; no
 1563:   multiple-maximal-component extension is asserted here.
 1564: \end{lemma}
 1565: 
 1566: \begin{proof}
 1567:   Since \(\mathcal N\) is trim and strongly connected, \(B_N\) is an
 1568:   irreducible non-negative matrix. The periodic Perron--Frobenius
 1569:   theorem therefore gives
 1570:   \[
 1571:     B_N^m
 1572:     =\lambda^m\Bigl(\sum_{\ell=0}^{d_N-1}\omega_{d_N}^{\ell m}E_\ell+R_m\Bigr),
 1573:     \qquad \|R_m\|\le C\theta_N^m
 1574:   \]
 1575:   for some spectral projectors \(E_\ell\), constant \(C>0\), and
 1576:   \(\theta_N\in(0,1)\), where \(\omega_{d_N}:=e^{2\pi i/d_N}\).
 1577:   Equivalently, on cyclic classes \(C_i,C_j\), if
 1578:   \(h\equiv j-i\pmod {d_N}\) and \(x\in C_i,y\in C_j\), then the
 1579:   irreducible periodic Perron--Frobenius entry asymptotic gives
 1580:   \[
 1581:     \lambda^{-(kd_N+h)}(B_N^{kd_N+h})_{xy}
 1582:       \longrightarrow h_y\nu_x>0
 1583:   \]
 1584:   for Perron vectors \(h,\nu>0\), normalized on the corresponding cyclic
 1585:   classes.
 1586:   For \(0\le r<d_N\) set
 1587:   \[
 1588:     S_r:=\sum_{\ell=0}^{d_N-1}\omega_{d_N}^{\ell r}E_\ell
 1589:         =\lim_{k\to\infty}\lambda^{-(kd_N+r)}B_N^{kd_N+r}.
 1590:   \]
 1591:   Each matrix in the limit is non-negative, so every entry of \(S_r\) is
 1592:   non-negative. Grouping the expansion by the residue class of \(m\)
 1593:   yields
 1594:   \[
 1595:     B_N^m=\lambda^m\bigl(S_{m\bmod d_N}+E_m\bigr),
 1596:     \qquad \|E_m\|\le C\theta_N^m.
 1597:   \]
 1598:   Let \(u_N\) and \(v_N\) be the indicator vectors of the initial and
 1599:   accepting states, respectively, and define
 1600:   \[
 1601:     d_r:=u_N^{\mathsf T}S_r v_N\ge 0.
 1602:   \]
 1603:   The constant \(d_r\) is positive exactly for the residue classes that
 1604:   contain arbitrarily long accepted words. Indeed, if
 1605:   \(d_r>0\), then some initial-to-accepting entry of \(S_r\) is
 1606:   positive; the convergence defining \(S_r\) gives
 1607:   \((B_N^{kd_N+r})_{q_N f}>0\) for all sufficiently large \(k\) and
 1608:   some \(f\in F_N\), hence accepted words of lengths \(kd_N+r\).
 1609:   Conversely, suppose that the residue class \(r\bmod d_N\) contains
 1610:   accepted words of arbitrarily large length. Then for infinitely many
 1611:   \(k\) there is an accepting state \(f_k\in F_N\) with
 1612:   \((B_N^{kd_N+r})_{q_N f_k}>0\). Since \(F_N\) is finite, one
 1613:   accepting state \(f\) occurs for infinitely many \(k\). In an
 1614:   irreducible non-negative matrix of period \(d_N\), the
 1615:   cyclic-class threshold in \Cref{lem:cyclic-class-path-threshold}
 1616:   applies, so \(q_N\) and \(f\) lie in cyclic classes whose difference
 1617:   is \(r\), and
 1618:   \((B_N^{kd_N+r})_{q_N f}>0\) for all sufficiently large \(k\).
 1619:   Applying the entry asymptotic displayed above with \(x=q_N\) and
 1620:   \(y=f\) gives \((S_r)_{q_N f}>0\), and therefore
 1621:   \(d_r=u_N^{\mathsf T}S_rv_N>0\).
 1622:   Substituting into the expansion gives
 1623:   \[
 1624:     z_m=u_N^{\mathsf T}B_N^m v_N
 1625:     =\lambda^m\bigl(d_{m\bmod d_N}+O(\theta_N^m)\bigr).
 1626:   \]
 1627: \end{proof}

 1629: For any deterministic automaton \(\mathcal A\) over \(\Sigma\) we write
 1630: \[
 1631:   a_m(\mathcal A,\mathcal N)
 1632:   :=\abs{L(\mathcal A)\cap\mathcal N_m}.
 1633: \]
 1634: 
 1635: \begin{lemma}[Substochastic product expansion]
 1636:   \label{lem:substochastic-product-expansion}
 1637:   Let \(\mathcal N\) be a trim strongly connected deterministic
 1638:   presentation with adjacency matrix \(B_N\), Perron root
 1639:   \(\lambda>1\), and Perron--Frobenius right eigenvector
 1640:   \(h\in\RR_{>0}^{Q_N}\). For every deterministic automaton
 1641:   \(\mathcal A\) over the same alphabet, complete or partial as in
 1642:   \Cref{def:trim-deterministic-presentation}, there exist an integer
 1643:   \(D'\ge 1\), non-negative constants \(e_0,\dots,e_{D'-1}\), and
 1644:   \(\eta\in(0,1)\) such that
 1645:   \[
 1646:     a_m(\mathcal A,\mathcal N)
 1647:     =\lambda^m\bigl(e_{m\bmod D'}+O(\eta^m)\bigr).
 1648:   \]
 1649:   This product-expansion lemma supplies the constants used in
 1650:   \Cref{thm:parry-density} for fixed trim strongly connected
 1651:   presentations. The broader multicomponent finite-budget comparison is
 1652:   \Cref{thm:multicomponent-finite-budget}.
 1653: \end{lemma}
 1654: 
 1655: \begin{proof}
 1656:   If necessary, complete \(\mathcal A\) by adjoining a sink state; this
 1657:   leaves \(L(\mathcal A)\cap L(\mathcal N)\) unchanged. Form the
 1658:   synchronous product automaton of
 1659:   \(\mathcal B=\mathcal N\times\mathcal A\) and trim it by deleting
 1660:   states that are unreachable from the initial pair or cannot reach an
 1661:   accepting pair. If no state remains, then
 1662:   \(a_m(\mathcal A,\mathcal N)=0\) for all \(m\), and the assertion
 1663:   holds with \(D'=1\) and \(e_0=0\). Otherwise let \(Q'\) be the state
 1664:   set of the resulting product \(\mathcal B'\), let \(B'\) be its
 1665:   adjacency matrix, and let \(u'\) and \(v'\) be the indicator vectors
 1666:   of its initial and accepting states. Trimming does not change the
 1667:   intersection counts, so
 1668:   \[
 1669:     a_m(\mathcal A,\mathcal N)=u'^{\mathsf T}B'^m v'.
 1670:   \]
 1671: 
 1672:   Let \(\pi\colon Q'\to Q_N\) forget the \(\mathcal A\)-coordinate.
 1673:   Define \(\widetilde h_x:=h_{\pi(x)}\), put
 1674:   \(\widetilde D:=\operatorname{diag}(\widetilde h)\), and set
 1675:   \[
 1676:     P':=\lambda^{-1}\widetilde D^{-1}B'\widetilde D.
 1677:   \]
 1678:   For a state \(x=(q,s)\in Q'\),
 1679:   \[
 1680:     \sum_{y\in Q'}P'_{xy}
 1681:     =\frac{1}{\lambda h_q}\sum_{y\in Q'}B'_{xy}h_{\pi(y)}.
 1682:   \]
 1683:   Because the product is deterministic letter by letter, each letter
 1684:   available from \(q\) in \(\mathcal N\) contributes to at most one
 1685:   outgoing edge from \(x\) in the product automaton, and trimming can
 1686:   only delete such edges. Hence
 1687:   \[
 1688:     \sum_{y\in Q'}B'_{xy}h_{\pi(y)}
 1689:     \le \sum_{\substack{q\xrightarrow{a}q'\\ \text{in }\mathcal N}} h_{q'}
 1690:     =(B_Nh)_q
 1691:     =\lambda h_q.
 1692:   \]
 1693:   Thus \(P'\) is substochastic.
 1694: 
 1695:   Adjoin a cemetery state \(\partial\) and define
 1696:   \[
 1697:     \widehat P:=
 1698:     \begin{pmatrix}
 1699:       P' & \mathbf{1}-P'\mathbf{1}\\
 1700:       0 & 1
 1701:     \end{pmatrix}.
 1702:   \]
 1703:   The matrix \(\widehat P\) is stochastic, and
 1704:   \((\widehat P^m)_{xy}=(P'^m)_{xy}\) for all \(x,y\in Q'\). Apply the
 1705:   finite Markov-chain canonical decomposition to \(\widehat P\). After
 1706:   permuting states, write
 1707:   \[
 1708:     \widehat P=
 1709:     \begin{pmatrix}
 1710:       T & R_1 & \cdots & R_s\\
 1711:       0 & C_1 & 0 & 0\\
 1712:       \vdots & 0 & \ddots & 0\\
 1713:       0 & 0 & 0 & C_s
 1714:     \end{pmatrix},
 1715:   \]
 1716:   where \(T\) is the transient block, \(\rho(T)<1\), and each \(C_j\) is
 1717:   an irreducible stochastic recurrent class with period \(d_j\). For
 1718:   \(m\ge1\),
 1719:   \[
 1720:     \widehat P^m=
 1721:     \begin{pmatrix}
 1722:       T^m &
 1723:       \sum_{\ell=0}^{m-1}T^\ell R_1C_1^{m-1-\ell} &
 1724:       \cdots &
 1725:       \sum_{\ell=0}^{m-1}T^\ell R_sC_s^{m-1-\ell}\\
 1726:       0 & C_1^m & 0 & 0\\
 1727:       \vdots & 0 & \ddots & 0\\
 1728:       0 & 0 & 0 & C_s^m
 1729:     \end{pmatrix}.
 1730:   \]
 1731:   The powers \(T^\ell\) decay exponentially, while each \(C_j^m\) has
 1732:   the usual periodic Perron--Frobenius limits. Hence, with
 1733:   \(D'=\operatorname{lcm}(d_1,\dots,d_s)\), the entrywise limits
 1734:   \[
 1735:     S_r:=\lim_{k\to\infty}P'^{kD'+r}
 1736:     \qquad(0\le r<D')
 1737:   \]
 1738:   exist on the \(Q'\times Q'\) block. These limits include the
 1739:   non-decaying absorption terms from transient states into recurrent
 1740:   classes. Since convergence of \(T^\ell\) is exponential and the
 1741:   non-peripheral parts of the recurrent blocks decay exponentially,
 1742:   there are a constant \(C>0\) and \(\eta\in(0,1)\) such that
 1743:   \[
 1744:     P'^m=S_{m\bmod D'}+E_m,
 1745:     \qquad
 1746:     \|E_m\|\le C\eta^m.
 1747:   \]
 1748:   The residue matrices are non-negative because they are entrywise
 1749:   limits of non-negative matrices. This also covers the case in which
 1750:   the restricted block is purely transient, where every \(S_r\) is the
 1751:   zero matrix.
 1752: 
 1753:   Since \(B'^m=\lambda^m\widetilde DP'^m\widetilde D^{-1}\), we obtain
 1754:   \[
 1755:     a_m(\mathcal A,\mathcal N)
 1756:     =\lambda^m\widetilde u^{\mathsf T}P'^m\widetilde v,
 1757:     \qquad
 1758:     \widetilde u:=\widetilde D u',
 1759:     \quad
 1760:     \widetilde v:=\widetilde D^{-1}v'.
 1761:   \]
 1762:   Therefore
 1763:   \[
 1764:     a_m(\mathcal A,\mathcal N)
 1765:     =\lambda^m\bigl(e_{m\bmod D'}+O(\eta^m)\bigr),
 1766:     \qquad
 1767:     e_r:=\widetilde u^{\mathsf T}S_r\widetilde v\ge 0,
 1768:   \]
 1769:   as required.
 1770: \end{proof}
 1771: 
 1772: \begin{theorem}[Background relative density for a trim strongly connected presentation]
 1773:   \label{thm:parry-density}
 1774:   Let \(\mathcal N\) be a trim strongly connected deterministic
 1775:   presentation in the sense of
 1776:   \Cref{def:trim-deterministic-presentation}, with Perron root
 1777:   \(\lambda>1\), and let
 1778:   \(\mathcal A\) be a deterministic automaton over \(\Sigma\). Then
 1779:   there exist an integer \(D_N\ge 1\), non-negative constants
 1780:   \(c_0,\dots,c_{D_N-1}\), and \(\theta\in(0,1)\) such that for all
 1781:   sufficiently large \(m\) with \(z_m>0\),
 1782:   \[
 1783:     \frac{a_m(\mathcal A,\mathcal N)}{z_m}
 1784:     =c_{m\bmod D_N}+O(\theta^m).
 1785:   \]
 1786:   In particular, either the ratio
 1787:   \(a_m(\mathcal A,\mathcal N)/z_m\) decays exponentially fast, or else
 1788:   it stays bounded below by a positive constant along an arithmetic
 1789:   progression of lengths that contains infinitely many indices with
 1790:   \(z_m>0\).
 1791:   This theorem is a background conditional-density tool for the stated
 1792:   trim strongly connected deterministic setting; the new finite-budget
 1793:   use of it is isolated in
 1794:   \Cref{cor:relative-finite-budget-obstruction}.
 1795: \end{theorem}
 1796: 
 1797: \begin{proof}
 1798:   This is the standard conditional-density conclusion for deterministic
 1799:   presentations, specialized to our notation; compare
 1800:   \cite{HanselPerrin1989,Kozik2005Conditional,Koga2019Density,Montoya2025Relative,BertheGouletPerrin2025}.
 1801:   The proof below is included only to identify the constants used later:
 1802:   \Cref{lem:substochastic-product-expansion} supplies the product
 1803:   expansion, and \Cref{lem:trim-density} supplies the positive
 1804:   denominator constants on relevant residue classes.
 1805:   Let \(h\in\RR_{>0}^{Q_N}\) be a Perron--Frobenius right eigenvector of
 1806:   \(B_N\). By \Cref{lem:substochastic-product-expansion}, there are
 1807:   \(D'\ge 1\), non-negative constants \(e_0,\dots,e_{D'-1}\), and
 1808:   \(\eta\in(0,1)\) such that
 1809:   \[
 1810:     a_m(\mathcal A,\mathcal N)
 1811:     =\lambda^m\bigl(e_{m\bmod D'}+O(\eta^m)\bigr).
 1812:   \]
 1813: 
 1814:   Now combine this with \Cref{lem:trim-density}. After replacing \(D'\)
 1815:   by a common multiple \(D_N\) of \(D'\) and \(d_N\), and regrouping the
 1816:   residue classes, there exist non-negative constants
 1817:   \(e_0,\dots,e_{D_N-1}\), \(d_0,\dots,d_{D_N-1}\), and \(\theta\in(0,1)\)
 1818:   such that
 1819:   \[
 1820:     a_m(\mathcal A,\mathcal N)
 1821:     =\lambda^m\bigl(e_{m\bmod D_N}+O(\theta^m)\bigr),
 1822:     \qquad
 1823:     z_m=\lambda^m\bigl(d_{m\bmod D_N}+O(\theta^m)\bigr).
 1824:   \]
 1825:   If \(z_m>0\) for infinitely many \(m\equiv r\pmod {D_N}\), then
 1826:   \Cref{lem:trim-density} gives \(d_r>0\). Along every such residue
 1827:   class,
 1828:   \[
 1829:     \frac{a_m(\mathcal A,\mathcal N)}{z_m}
 1830:     =\frac{e_r+O(\theta^m)}{d_r+O(\theta^m)}
 1831:     =\frac{e_r}{d_r}+O(\theta^m).
 1832:   \]
 1833:   Setting \(c_r:=e_r/d_r\) on residue classes with \(d_r>0\) proves the
 1834:   stated expansion for all sufficiently large \(m\) with \(z_m>0\).
 1835: 
 1836:   Finally, if every relevant \(e_r\) vanishes, then
 1837:   \(a_m(\mathcal A,\mathcal N)=O((\lambda\theta)^m)\) on every residue
 1838:   class with \(z_m>0\), so the ratio decays exponentially. Otherwise
 1839:   some relevant \(e_r\) is positive, and along the corresponding
 1840:   arithmetic progression the ratio stays bounded below by a positive
 1841:   constant.
 1842: \end{proof}
 1843: 
 1844: Only the following finite-budget consequence is used in the prime-slice
 1845: applications.
 1846: It is the exact form of the background relative-density theorem needed
 1847: below, after the substochastic product expansion and the positive
 1848: periodic denominator constants have already been supplied in
 1849: \Cref{lem:substochastic-product-expansion,lem:trim-density}.
 1850: 
 1851: \begin{corollary}[Finite-budget lemma for a trim presentation]
 1852:   \label{cor:relative-finite-budget-obstruction}
 1853:   Let \(\mathcal N\) and \(\mathcal A\) satisfy the hypotheses of
 1854:   \Cref{thm:parry-density}. For each \(m\) with \(z_m>0\), let
 1855:   \(T_m\subseteq\mathcal N_m\). Suppose that there are constants
 1856:   \(\alpha,\beta>0\) such that, for all sufficiently large \(m\) with
 1857:   \(z_m>0\),
 1858:   \[
 1859:     \alpha\,\frac{\lambda^m}{m}
 1860:     \le \abs{T_m}
 1861:     \le \beta\,\frac{\lambda^m}{m}.
 1862:   \]
 1863:   Put \(A_m:=L(\mathcal A)\cap\mathcal N_m\). Then there is a constant
 1864:   \(C_{\mathcal A,\mathcal N,T}>0\) such that
 1865:   \[
 1866:     \abs{A_m\triangle T_m}
 1867:     \ge C_{\mathcal A,\mathcal N,T}\,\frac{\lambda^m}{m}
 1868:   \]
 1869:   for all sufficiently large \(m\) with \(z_m>0\).
 1870: 
 1871:   More precisely, after passing to the residue classes supplied by
 1872:   \Cref{thm:parry-density}, every relevant residue class has one of the
 1873:   following two behaviours. If its limiting relative-density constant
 1874:   is zero, then
 1875:   \[
 1876:     \frac{\abs{A_m\cap T_m}}{\abs{T_m}}
 1877:     \le \frac{\abs{A_m}}{\abs{T_m}}
 1878:   \]
 1879:   decays exponentially along that residue class. If its limiting
 1880:   relative-density constant is positive, then along that residue class
 1881:   \[
 1882:     \abs{A_m\triangle T_m}\gg \lambda^m,
 1883:     \qquad
 1884:     \frac{\abs{A_m\cap T_m}}{\abs{A_m}}=O(1/m)
 1885:   \]
 1886:   whenever the second ratio is defined.
 1887: \end{corollary}
 1888: 
 1889: \begin{proof}
 1890:   Let \(D_N\), \(c_0,\dots,c_{D_N-1}\), and \(\theta\in(0,1)\) be supplied
 1891:   by \Cref{thm:parry-density}. Enlarge \(D_N\), if necessary, so that it
 1892:   is also a multiple of the period in \Cref{lem:trim-density}. Then for
 1893:   every residue class \(r\bmod D_N\) containing infinitely many lengths
 1894:   with \(z_m>0\), there is a constant \(d_r>0\) such that
 1895:   \[
 1896:     z_m=\lambda^m(d_r+O(\theta^m))
 1897:     \qquad (m\equiv r\bmod {D_N}),
 1898:   \]
 1899:   after increasing \(\theta\) within \((0,1)\) if needed. Hence
 1900:   \(z_m\asymp\lambda^m\)
 1901:   on each relevant residue class.
 1902: 
 1903:   Fix such a residue class. If \(c_r=0\), then
 1904:   \(\abs{A_m}/z_m=O(\theta^m)\), and therefore
 1905:   \[
 1906:     \abs{A_m}=O(\lambda^m\theta^m).
 1907:   \]
 1908:   Choosing \(\eta\) with \(\theta<\eta<1\), the elementary bound
 1909:   \(m\theta^m=O(\eta^m)\) gives
 1910:   \[
 1911:     \frac{\abs{A_m\cap T_m}}{\abs{T_m}}
 1912:     \le \frac{\abs{A_m}}{\abs{T_m}}
 1913:     =O(m\theta^m)
 1914:     =O(\eta^m),
 1915:   \]
 1916:   so recall against \(T_m\) decays exponentially on this residue class.
 1917:   Also, for all sufficiently large \(m\) in this class,
 1918:   \[
 1919:     \abs{A_m\triangle T_m}
 1920:     \ge \abs{T_m}-\abs{A_m}
 1921:     \ge \frac{\alpha}{2}\,\frac{\lambda^m}{m}.
 1922:   \]
 1923: 
 1924:   If \(c_r>0\), then \(\abs{A_m}/z_m\ge c_r/2\) for all sufficiently
 1925:   large \(m\equiv r\bmod {D_N}\) with \(z_m>0\). Since
 1926:   \(z_m\asymp\lambda^m\) on the residue class, there is a constant
 1927:   \(\gamma_r>0\) such that \(\abs{A_m}\ge\gamma_r\lambda^m\). The upper
 1928:   bound on \(\abs{T_m}\) then gives, for all sufficiently large \(m\) in
 1929:   the class,
 1930:   \[
 1931:     \abs{A_m\triangle T_m}
 1932:     \ge \abs{A_m}-\abs{T_m}
 1933:     \ge \frac{\gamma_r}{2}\lambda^m,
 1934:   \]
 1935:   and, whenever \(\abs{A_m}>0\),
 1936:   \[
 1937:     \frac{\abs{A_m\cap T_m}}{\abs{A_m}}
 1938:     \le \frac{\abs{T_m}}{\abs{A_m}}
 1939:     \le \frac{\beta}{\gamma_r}\,\frac{1}{m}.
 1940:   \]
 1941: 
 1942:   There are only finitely many relevant residue classes. Taking the
 1943:   minimum of the positive constants obtained above proves the uniform
 1944:   lower bound \(C_{\mathcal A,\mathcal N,T}\lambda^m/m\) for all
 1945:   sufficiently large \(m\) with \(z_m>0\), and the two residue-class
 1946:   alternatives prove the remaining assertions.
 1947: \end{proof}
 1948: 
 1949: \noindent
 1950: This finite-budget lemma is the only relative-density consequence used
 1951: below: the base-\(b\) and Zeckendorf prime slices are exactly the
 1952: instances in which \(T_m\) has size comparable to \(\lambda^m/m\) by
 1953: \Cref{lem:base-prime-count} and \artref{Lemma~2.5}.
 1954: 
 1955: \begin{remark}
 1956:   When \(\mathcal N\) is the trim strongly connected presentation of a
 1957:   Parry numeration system or of the Zeckendorf language, the same
 1958:   presentation-level statement applies with \(\lambda\) equal to the
 1959:   dominant root of the corresponding recurrence. Presentations with
 1960:   multiple maximal components are covered by
 1961:   \Cref{thm:multicomponent-finite-budget}, where polynomial factors are
 1962:   retained. Nondeterministic or weighted presentations are not treated
 1963:   here; see \cite{CharlierRampersadRigoWaxweiler2010} for examples where
 1964:   multicomponent behaviour genuinely occurs.
 1965: \end{remark}
 1966: 
 1967: \begin{remark}[Relation to conditional-density literature]
 1968:   Classical treatments of densities of rational languages already appear
 1969:   in Hansel and Perrin~\cite{HanselPerrin1989} and in the conditional
 1970:   and relative-density analyses of Kozik~\cite{Kozik2005Conditional},
 1971:   Koga \cite{Koga2019Density}, Montoya \cite{Montoya2025Relative}, and
 1972:   Berth\'e--Goulet-Ouellet--Perrin \cite{BertheGouletPerrin2025}.
 1973:   Thus \Cref{thm:dfa-density-dichotomy,thm:parry-density} are used here
 1974:   as standard inputs for the fixed-DFA and strongly connected
 1975:   deterministic settings. The multicomponent theorem keeps the
 1976:   polynomial factors that those inputs suppress. The contribution is
 1977:   the conversion of these residue-class expansions into the
 1978:   finite-budget prime obstructions recorded in
 1979:   \Cref{thm:multicomponent-finite-budget,cor:relative-finite-budget-obstruction,cor:dfa-prime-symmetric-diff,cor:dfa-prime-recall-precision}.
 1980: \end{remark}
 1981:

codex
The Evertse citation does support the manuscript’s use: Theorem 3 treats ratios \(u_r/u_s\) of a nondegenerate recurrence with at least two characteristic roots and forces unbounded prime-ideal support. After the manuscript’s standard arithmetic-progression decomposition, the deduction of a one-root geometric subray is mathematically plausible; the scripts only test finite examples and do not validate this Diophantine step.

                                                                                             1. Introduction
  
>                                            Multiple context-free languages were introduced by Seki, Matsumura, Fujii 
and Kasami [25,
                                          37]. They were proposed as an attempt to describe the syntax of natural 
languages (see for
                                          example [6]), but were later shown not to suffice when Salvati proved that 
the language MIX3
                                          is multiple context-free [36], since MIX3 is regarded as a language that 
should not appear in any
                                          class capturing the syntax of natural languages [17].
  
                                             A useful tool for working with formal language classes is to find a 
necessary condition for
                                          a language to belong to the class. For example, the well-known pumping 
lemmas for regular
                                          and context-free languages (see for example [38]), Ogden's lemma (see Lemma 
5.5) and the
                                          Interchange lemma for context-free languages [33, 34], Gilman's Shrinking 
lemma for indexed
                                          languages [13], Mitrana and Stiebe's Interchange lemma and the Swapping 
lemma of the second
                                          author for blind multi-counter languages [30, 10].
  
>                                            Seki et al. [37] gave what was later called a weak pumping lemma for 
multiple context-free
                                          languages, which is weak in the sense that pumping only applies to a single 
word in the language,
>                                         rather than all words that are sufficiently long (see Lemma 5.3). Kanazawa 
et al. [23] proved that
                                          it was not possible to prove a certain version of the standard pumping lemma 
for context-free
                                          languages to multiple context-free languages, and Kanazawa also showed a 
variant of generalised
                                          Ogden's lemma is not possible [22]. Meanwhile, attempts have also been made 
to prove stronger
                                          versions of both lemmas for some subclasses of multiple context-free 
languages (for example, for
                                          well-nested multiple context-free languages there is a pumping lemma [21], 
strengthened and
                                          accompanied with Ogden's lemma in [39]).
  
                                             In this article we introduce a necessary condition for an infinite 
language to be multiple
                                          context-free, which we call a Substitution Lemma (Theorem 4.5), as an 
alternative type of pump-
                                          ing lemma for multiple context-free languages, which is strong in the sense 
that the substitution

  5.1. The word problem of F2�F2. Recall that the word problem for a group G with generating
  set X, denoted WP (G, X), is the set of words in X  X-1  which equal the identity element
  of the group (where X-1 = {x-1 | x  X} contains the inverse element for each x  X). Since
  multiple context-free languages are closed under inverse homomorphism (Proposition 2.3 (3)),
  having multiple context-free word problem is independent of choice of finite generating set.
  Salvati's result shows that the word problem of Z2 is 2-multiple context-free (see also [32, 5]). Ho
  [16] extended this to show that Zn is k-multiple context-free for some k > n, and later Gebhardt
  et al. [11] sharpened this by showing that in fact the word problem of Zn is n-multiple context-
  free. Since having a multiple context-free word problem is closed under finite index supergroup

  452: \begin{proof}
  453:   If neither alternative held, finiteness of \(S\) would give
  454:   \(K\ge0\) and \(E\in\NN_0^S\) such that
  455:   \[
  456:     \{\val_U(w):w\in L\}\subseteq X_{K,E}.
  457:   \]
  458:   By \Cref{prop:local-prime-factor-cb-rank}, \(X_{K,E}\) is scattered.
  459:   This contradicts
  460:   \Cref{thm:mcfl-local-adic-fingerprint}. Prime values satisfy
  461:   \(\omega_{S^c}\le1\) and \(v_p\le1\); bounded \(\Omega\) bounds both
  462:   alternatives; and finite prime support bounds \(\omega_{S^c}\), with
  463:   the remaining valuations bounded by hypothesis. If \(S=\varnothing\),
  464:   the second alternative is absent, giving the unit-system assertion.
  465: \end{proof}
  466: 
  467: The second alternative is necessary. In ordinary base \(b\), where
  468: \(a_0=b\), the regular LSD-first language
  469: \(\{0^n1:n\ge0\}\) represents \(b^n\). Its distinct prime support is
  470: fixed, while \(v_p(b^n)\) is unbounded for every \(p\mid b\).

  472: \begin{proposition}[Recurrence-witness inflation and strict separation]
  473:   \label{prop:recurrence-witness-separation}
  474:   If a tail has minimal recurrence polynomial \(\mu_U\), then for every
  475:   prime \(p\) it also has a recurrence witness with characteristic
  476:   polynomial \((X-p)\mu_U(X)\).  When \(\abs{\mu_U(0)}=1\), the trailing
  477:   coefficient of this witness has absolute value \(p\).
  478: 
  479:   Moreover, there are two canonical eventually recurrent
  480:   numeration systems with regular representation languages and recurrence
  481:   witnesses whose trailing-coefficient prime set is \(\{p\}\), but with
  482:   opposite bounded-outside-prime escape behavior:
  483:   \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
  484:     \item ordinary base \(p\) contains the infinite regular language
  485:     \(\{0^n1:n\ge0\}\), whose values are \(p^n\);
  486:     \item the Zeckendorf system, equipped with the order-three recurrence
  487:     witness
  488:     \[
  489:       F_{n+3}=-pF_n+(1-p)F_{n+1}+(p+1)F_{n+2},
  490:     \]
  491:     contains no infinite MCFL \(L\) for which
  492:     \[
  493:       \sup_{w\in L}\omega_{\{p\}^c}(\val(w))<\infty.
  494:     \]
  495:   \end{enumerate}
  496:   Thus the prime divisors of an arbitrarily selected trailing coefficient
  497:   do not determine the escape behavior of the numeration system.
  498: \end{proposition}
  499: 
  500: \begin{proof}
  501:   The polynomial identity \(\mu_U(C)z_J=0\) remains valid after
  502:   multiplication by \(X-p\).  In the companion convention, the trailing
  503:   recurrence coefficient is the negative of the constant term of the
  504:   characteristic polynomial, proving the first assertion.
  505: 
  506:   The base-\(p\) assertion is the preceding example.  For the Zeckendorf
  507:   sequence, multiplication of its minimal polynomial by \(X-p\) gives
  508:   \[
  509:     (X-p)(X^2-X-1)
  510:       =X^3-(p+1)X^2+(p-1)X+p,
  511:   \]
  512:   which is exactly the displayed recurrence and has trailing coefficient
  513:   \(-p\).  This changes neither the sequence nor its regular canonical
  514:   representation language.  On the other hand, its minimal recurrence
  515:   has unit trailing coefficient.  If the displayed supremum were bounded
  516:   by \(K\), then
  517:   \(\omega(\val(w))\le K+1\) on \(L\), contrary to the unit-recurrence
  518:   conclusion of
  519:   \Cref{thm:nonunit-mcfl-escape-dichotomy}.  This proves the separation.
  520: \end{proof}

  316:   Fixed-base prime CF-immunity is classical. Hartmanis and Shank proved
  317:   that no infinite set of primes can be accepted in fixed-base notation
  318:   by a pushdown automaton; Sch\"utzenberger obtained the conclusion
  319:   independently \cite{HartmanisShank1968,Schutzenberger1968}. We do not
  320:   reproduce their proofs as new. Our use of Ogden's lemma
  321:   \cite{Ogden1968} instead couples the two pumped blocks to the
  322:   Zeckendorf unimodular action and yields the stronger coprime-quotient
  323:   chain
  324:   \Cref{thm:context-free-coprime-quotient-zeckendorf-pumping}. The
  325:   weak pumping lemma of Seki--Matsumura--Fujii--Kasami
  326:   \cite{SekiEtAl1991} supplies one synchronized \(2k\)-block orbit for
  327:   every infinite \(k\)-MCFL; it is used as an input, not reproved.
  328:   Kanazawa--Kobele--Michaelis--Salvati--Yoshinaka prove that the usual
  329:   strong pumping form fails in general
  330:   \cite{KanazawaKobeleMichaelisSalvatiYoshinaka2014}, and the recent
  331:   substitution lemma of Duncan--Elder--Frenkel--Liu gives a different
  332:   strong interface \cite{DuncanElderFrenkelLiu2026}. Neither result
  333:   concerns recurrence numeration or divisibility. The new deductions
  334:   are the fixed local-congruence orbit
  335:   \Cref{thm:mcfl-synchronized-congruence-orbit}, the topological
  336:   fingerprint \Cref{thm:mcfl-local-adic-fingerprint}, the exact rank
  337:   formula \Cref{prop:local-prime-factor-cb-rank}, and the escape
  338:   dichotomy \Cref{thm:nonunit-mcfl-escape-dichotomy}. The unit-system
  339:   constructions are \Cref{thm:unit-mcfl-deep-congruence-chain} and
  340:   \Cref{thm:unit-mcfl-divisibility-tree}.
  341:   Evertse's theorem on prime ideals in ratios of terms of
  342:   nondegenerate recurrences \cite{Evertse1984} is used as an arithmetic
  343:   input to the geometric-ray characterization
  344:   \Cref{thm:bounded-outside-support-geometric-ray}; it is not claimed as
  345:   a new recurrence theorem.
  346:   Broughan's \(\mathbb Q\)- and Cantor-space classifications for adic
  347:   integer topologies are cited as classical inputs
  348:   \cite{Broughan2003}. Frougny normalization and the
  349:   Bertrand/substitution literature
  350:   \cite{Frougny1992,BruyereHansel1997,Fabre1995,FrougnySolomyak1992}
  351:   supply the canonical finite-state numeration interface, not the
  352:   arithmetic pumping proof. The residual nonunit and non-positional
  353:   limits are stated in \Cref{rem:pisot-open-interfaces}. The
  354:   recurrence-witness separation
  355:   \Cref{prop:recurrence-witness-separation} distinguishes the invariant
  356:   minimal action from an arbitrarily inflated companion presentation.
  357:

  359:   \suppref{Theorem~A.1} is the usual
  360:   P\'olya--Carlson natural-boundary mechanism for Euler products.
  361:   \suppref{Proposition~A.2} is the corresponding
  362:   periodicity obstruction for determinant models after \(z=e^{-s}\). Both are
  363:   classical
  364:   \cite{Polya1923,Carlson1921,Estermann1928,ArtinMazur1965,BowenLanford1970}.
